book_growth.why: Common equity was about $30.3bn at September 30, 2026, up about 6% from $28.6bn. Earnings were largely offset by buybacks, dividends and a swing to unrealised losses. Buybacks are running at more than three times the prior-year pace. Growth should stay well below the return on equity because most earnings are paid out, so I assume 4-5% a year once income normalises.

fade_years.why: The return needs a long fade, because it must come down from a peak near 40% to about 14% as the hard market softens. A 10-year fade is a middle estimate for a cyclical personal-lines business.

situation.roe_position: The 2025 return of 52% and the 12-month return of 41% to September 2026 are far above normal for a personal-lines insurer. They reflect a hard-market margin recovery after the 2022-23 losses: rate increases pushed the combined ratio to about 85. Large prior-year reserve releases, higher investment income and a base year with disposition gains added to it. The opening equity base is also small because of the earlier loss years. The return should fade as rates, reserve releases and catastrophe losses normalise.
situation.why: 2025 income to common of $10.2bn on opening common equity of $28.6bn is a cyclical peak. It includes disposition gains and $1.8bn of reserve releases, so it is not a through-cycle level. The company is returning capital quickly (nine-month buybacks of $2.9bn plus dividends) with flat debt, so equity growth is limited by payout choices, not regulatory capital. Subsidiary dividend limits and rate regulation remain background constraints.

book_growth.why: Common equity was about $30.3bn at September 30 versus $28.6bn at the 2025 year-end base. Buybacks ($2.9bn in nine months, against $0.8bn a year earlier) and dividends absorb most earnings, so growth is held to about 5-9% a year. Unrealized bond losses also reduced equity in 2026.

fade_years.why: The excess-return fade from about 16% to 14% is gradual because the franchise has scale and growing policy counts, but competition and rate regulation erode it over roughly a decade.

The filed history shows a median of about 5% and a swing from negative to 52%, and auto and homeowners margins move with the catastrophe, inflation and rate-approval cycle. I use about 14%, above the 9.4% cost of equity because scale, a low-cost position and investment income support some excess return, but well below the current level. State profit limits and competition cap it.

terminal_growth.why: Growth is anchored near nominal GDP. Policies in force are growing about 3-4% and premiums are rising with inflation, but a mature market share and heavy payout limit book growth beyond the fade.

risks.risk: Underwriting margins normalize faster: heavier catastrophe losses, fewer reserve releases and auto severity or rate regulation squeeze the combined ratio.
Unrealized bond losses and a hard-market reversal cut earnings and slow equity growth, while buybacks still drain capital.

situation.roe_position: Reported ROE is very high because the personal auto and homeowners underwriting cycle is near its peak. Combined ratios are in the mid-80s, there are large prior-year reserve releases, and net investment income is rising. The 2025 base year also includes disposition gains. The ROE is on a common equity base that was depressed by 2022-2023 losses, so it flatters the long-run level. I expect it to fade as rates normalize, reserve releases shrink, catastrophe losses revert and equity compounds.
situation.why: The 2025 ROE of 52% rests on a 2022-23 loss-depleted equity base, $1.5bn of disposition gains and $1.8bn of reserve releases, so it is not a run-rate. Capital does not appear to limit book growth: nine-month buybacks of $2.9bn plus dividends were funded from $10.0bn of operating cash flow with flat debt. Book equity growth is therefore set by earnings less a near-full payout, not by regulatory capital. Parent deployable capital and statutory surplus are not shown in the packet, so that conclusion carries some uncertainty.
